title: Urban land use, urban problems and their answers

blocks.heading: What this section covers
blocks.text: What land use in a city looks like and why it sorts into zones; the problems cities develop, their causes and the solutions tried against them.

blocks.heading: The zones of land use
blocks.text: A city's land use sorts into zones, and the names matter. The CBD, the Central Business District, is the commercial centre: the shops, offices, banks and civic buildings around the main street, where land values are highest. Around and beyond it lie the inner-city areas, older and denser housing built when workers had to walk to work. Further out lie the suburbs, newer housing at lower density with gardens and space, which spread as trams, buses and cars freed people from walking. At the edge lies the rural-urban fringe, the zone where urban and rural land uses meet: smallholdings, market gardens, new housing estates, warehouses and open land awaiting the city's arrival.

blocks.heading: Why the land use sorts as it does
blocks.text: The sorting has a mechanism behind it: accessibility. The centre of a city is the one point the whole urban area can reach most easily, so businesses compete for it, and their bidding pushes land values to their highest point. Whoever pays those values builds high and uses every floor, which is why CBDs rise into high-rise offices and shops and hold little else; a car park or a wheat field on the busiest corner cannot pay its rent. Further out, land is cheaper and travel slower, so the uses that need space, houses with gardens, warehouses, factories, take the ground instead. Describing a CBD means naming what stands there, high offices, shops, banks, little open space; explaining it means giving the mechanism, highest accessibility, so highest values, so highest buildings.

blocks.heading: Land use changes
blocks.text: The zones are a snapshot of a moving process. Cities grow outwards, so industry and new housing push into the rural-urban fringe and farmland gives way to estates; the suburbs of one generation become the inner city of the next as their housing ages; and trade itself moves, because a CBD can lose shoppers to out-of-town malls with free parking, leaving empty upper floors behind. So a land-use map always carries a date on it, and answers about change should name what is arriving and what it is arriving over.

blocks.heading: The problems and their causes
blocks.text: Urban problems grow from density and growth. Traffic congestion, because every trip converges on the same streets and the CBD's oldest streets were built narrowest. Housing shortage and squatter settlements, because in a fast-growing city the arrivals outnumber the homes built, so newcomers settle on land they do not own and build for themselves. Pressure on services, because water pipes, sewer lines and refuse rounds are sized for one population and then handed another. And the loss of farmland at the fringe, because a spreading city builds on exactly the land that used to feed it. Each problem names its cause, and an answer that names the mechanism earns its marks: congestion follows trips, shortage follows growth, service failure follows population outrunning pipes.

blocks.heading: The solutions
blocks.text: Every solution either manages the flow or adds the supply. For traffic, more road space, bypasses, ring roads, dual carriageways, redirects vehicles around the centre, while public transport moves more people per road-space than private cars, so bus priority and rapid transit cut congestion with the same tarmac. For housing, three tools: servicing land with water, roads and power so that new settlement builds on prepared ground; upgrading existing settlements in place rather than clearing them; and self-help schemes, in which households build their own homes with organised support. For the fringe, green belts and planned expansion boundaries hold the city's shape. Every solution trades costs against reach, so an answer should say which family it belongs to and what it gives up.

blocks.heading: Where this connects
blocks.text: The zones here are the settlement hierarchy of topic 1.5 at the scale of one city; the growth that drives the problems is the urbanisation of topic 1.7; and Windhoek's growth carries the population dynamics of topic 1.1 into bricks.
